current_episode.title: Introducing The Jupiter Release of Galileo: An Inside Story

guest.bio_context: Josh Bersin has been studying human capital practices, management, and HR for close to 30 years, starting in 1998. Over this period, he has identified 95 functional capability areas of human capital and developed maturity models, benchmarks, assessments, and nearly 1,800 case studies. His company operates as a research, advisory services, education, and consulting firm focused on understanding how organizations manage and develop their people in relation to business outcomes.

context.transcript_excerpt: Today, I'm going to tell you the story of the Jupiter release of Galileo. And it's a slightly long story, but I think you'll find it interesting and educational and a little promotional, but not too much. So most of you know that the history of our business is research, advisory services, education, and consulting. And so going back to 1998, when I first started doing this, What we basically have been doing for close to 30 years is studying the human capital practices of management, leadership, human resources, and all of the related tools and technologies that allow companies to manage and grow their people. It started originally with training, and then we got into leadership development, and then we got into succession management and performance management and talent management and executive development and pay equity and diversity and inclusion and well-being and employee experience and the pandemic and org design and many, many other topics. And over this 28-year period, we identified 95 functional capability areas of human capital. And you could say they're functional capabilities of HR, but they're really functional capabilities of management in general. And in each of those 95 areas, we've developed maturity models, benchmarks where they're appropriate, assessments, and hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of case studies. And we have more than 1,800, almost 1,800 case studies. And the reason we've done all these case studies is the purpose of this research is to give you actionable solutions to problems in your industry, in your location, in your company size. If I tell you how Google or Walmart does performance management and you're a fast-growing tech company or a small retailer or a retail distribution company in the UK, it may not apply at all. I mean, it might be interesting and you might learn something from it, but it may not be relevant. You'd probably rather hear a story from a company like yours and what happened to them. And over the years, what we found is that the way to produce and monetize this IP is through what we called a research membership. This is a very common model that Gartner uses in other research companies where we take the research, we produce it into reports and models and frameworks and graphics. By the way, this includes analysis of vendors, which is more of a vendor analyst work, but we do the same thing for vendors. So we have pretty much the same examples and same process. We talk to vendor customers. We talk to the vendors. We track their roadmaps and their success in the market and so forth. So we're kind of business analysts from that standpoint and HR analysts and management analysts at the same time. Anyway, we produce these reports, spend a lot of time making them beautiful, writing them, editing them. It's actually quite fun if you like writing. But it's, you know, a business like a publishing business. And then we sell or have sold access to this library like a library card where you kind of just go in and read whatever you want. And, of course, over the last decade, this has turned into videos, podcasts, and then educational materials. Because what we found is that nobody reads everything. And everybody who's a consumer of our materials has a particular job. And they want to know what's relevant to that job. They don't want to know what everything else is going on in management and HR. So we needed to build search tools and subscription models that allowed us to sell access to this research to the appropriate people in a company. And that includes C-level executives all the way down to recruiters or L&D specialists or technical specialists who are buying and selling technology. And by the way, we also have a lot of clients who are consultants and vendors who are trying to keep up with the market, too. pending_qa.q: How has the business model for monetizing human capital research evolved over the past decade?
pending_qa.r: The Josh Bersin Company initially used a research membership model similar to Gartner, selling access to a library of reports, models, and frameworks. Over the last decade, this evolved into videos, podcasts, and educational materials because consumers need content relevant to their specific job, not everything in management and HR. The business now includes subscription models that deliver appropriate research to different roles—from C-level executives to recruiters, L&D specialists, and technology vendors.

pending_qa.q: What opportunity did the emergence of large language models like ChatGPT create for HR research organizations?
pending_qa.r: When ChatGPT came out, Bersin saw an opportunity to build a search engine where users could query an entire corpus of knowledge and get answers, then find supporting reports. This led to the creation of Galileo, initially called the co-pilot, which not only found information but could generate new content—building implementation plans, RFP checklists, hiring guides, and behavioral interview guides using the organization's intellectual property.

pending_qa.q: Why did the strategy shift from building a specialized AI agent to creating a portable intelligence layer across multiple platforms?
pending_qa.r: Customers indicated they already had AI platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Microsoft Copilot and wanted Galileo integrated there rather than as a separate tool. This led to deals with ServiceNow, SAP, Workday, and others. The shift revealed that Galileo's power was being constrained by individual platforms, and the real value came from interleaving Galileo's intelligence with company policies and human capital data.

pending_qa.q: What structural changes were made to optimize research content for AI consumption, and what is the Agent Ready Corpus?
pending_qa.r: The Josh Bersin Company realized their content, written like traditional books with introductions, tables of contents, and conclusions, was inefficient for AI. They built ARC (Agent Ready Corpus), a new architecture that extracts the essence of Galileo's data, chunks it into machine-readable form, and carefully indexes it with eight dimensions of tagging so LLMs can read it accurately without hallucinating or guessing. This approach eliminates unnecessary boilerplate and enables the AI to cite sources precisely.

pending_qa.q: What performance advantage does the optimized Agent Ready Corpus deliver compared to general-purpose language models?
pending_qa.r: The ARC corpus is 10 to 100 times more efficient at token usage for running complex HR questions compared to using ChatGPT or Claude alone. Benchmarking against 30 golden prompts—complex human capital questions—showed that general LLMs hallucinate and misattribute information, while the optimized corpus is fast, secure, reliable, predictable, truthful, and efficient, providing accurate answers by industry, company size, domain, and problem.

pending_qa.q: How does the Jupiter release integrate human capital intelligence with enterprise systems and business problem-solving?
pending_qa.r: Galileo Jupiter includes a layer that understands data models from SAP, Oracle, Workday, and HiBob, allowing users to ask questions that combine Galileo's intelligence with company-specific human capital data. It can answer questions like 'What is the span of control of our sales department?' and compare salaries to benchmarks. The system creates a chain of thought connecting business problems to human capital issues and solutions, embedded in the HR 2030 model.

pending_qa.q: What new data sources and benchmarks were added to Galileo to enhance its relevance for enterprise decision-making?
pending_qa.r: The Jupiter release added executive compensation data from Equilar, job titles and skills for every major position in every functional area, salary benchmarks from Wagescape and other sources covering approximately 120 countries, benchmarks on turnover, business practices, and hundreds of datasets on vendor market technologies and HR solutions. This creates a comprehensive intelligence layer for salary analysis, skills assessment, and vendor evaluation.

pending_qa.q: How does the Microsoft Copilot integration of Galileo leverage enterprise graph data to create personalized learning and coaching applications?
pending_qa.r: Microsoft Copilot's unique advantage is access to the Microsoft Graph, including emails, SharePoint, Viva Skills, and WorkIQ data. Users can ask the Copilot implementation of Galileo to analyze their emails over two years and identify top skills relative to a new project, then recommend learning paths. Clients have built personal management coaches that read prior week meetings, apply their own management rubric, and provide coaching on performance improvements, with Galileo informing these insights.

pending_qa.q: Why is the Jupiter release named after Jupyter, and what business transformation does it represent?
pending_qa.r: The Jupiter release is named after Jupyter because it represents one of the biggest projects and most exciting initiatives in Bersin's career. It transforms the 30 years of research, printing, layout, and design into a format perfectly readable by machines, enabling the AI to make completely accurate and detailed analysis. It shifts the business from publishing PDF reports to producing content in Agent Ready Corpus form available within hours, dramatically accelerating the delivery of human capital intelligence.
